rows.reason: Line 53 sets 'reluctance in his face' against 'alacrity in his heart'; the contrast correctly leads to the keen, willing feeling he hid. Form ok.
Line 73 ties 'covet' to making a thing 'difficult to attain'; the script draws wanting the thing from that and separates it from envying the owner. Form ok.
Line 23 pairs 'pause' with 'a moment's irresolution', and the look behind the door comes on lines 23-24; the script separates the hesitation (key) from the looking. Form ok.

Final sentence 'His question to the ghost is short and sharp, which is the other word' brings in the key's word 'sharp' itself; it is not taken from the text, and 'short' is not in line 78. It also says a question 'is' a word, which is muddled. It does not show how to reach 'sharp and cutting in what he says' or rule out the acid sense.
'skirted a / noisy stream' (lines 24-25), and lines 25-26 say 'Both road and stream wound up' the valley together; the script correctly reasons 'along beside it, not away from it'. Form ok.
Line 74 'draped in ivy' and line 75 a window 'broke through the dark veil'; the script correctly identifies the veil as the ivy. Form ok.
'As you please' plus 'an air of resignation' (line 22) and 'patient gravity' (lines 24-25) support putting up with something unwanted. Form ok.
His attempt to 'beguile her into conversation on some more pleasing subject' (lines 52-53), then 'But she was inexorable'; the script uses the 'But' to show she was not moved. Form ok.
'a short sardonic laugh' (line 28) and the belittling remark on line 29; the script separates the mocking (key) from the shortness (distractor). Form ok.

Lines 33-35: heat and dust 'lulled' his mind 'into complete oblivion as to his promise'; the script points to the promise he forgot, which leads to the key and sets the lulling apart as the cause. Form ok.

'He strode over it' comes straight after a sentence whose subject is Mark, but on line 20 it is Bevis who 'strode over the yielding sand'. 'it took the print' is not in the text, and the script keeps the focus on footprints, which is distractor C ('Marked with the prints'), without separating softness from the marks.

'till then so low and shelving, suddenly became steep' (lines 26-27): the 'till then ... suddenly' contrast with steep gives a low, gentle slope. The script sets the evidence out before the key. Form ok.
Line 45 'almost felt inclined to leave it and run round'; the script uses the action after the word to show wanting or being tempted, which rules out the slope and leaning senses. Form ok.
Line 32 'Clara's promise, which comforted her' and line 33 'depend upon it'; the script identifies 'it' as the promise, which leads to trusting it. Form ok.
Line 38 'could not suppress a sob. But she made an effort to control herself'; the script ties suppress to holding back the sob. Form ok.

The script ends 'So the word names a stretch of the card game', but nothing it cites shows cards: line 9 only says the discussion 'fell during the rubber'. The cards are on lines 7-8 and it never points there. Its evidence (talk stopped, then resumed after) fits distractor C, 'A pause in which nobody spoke', just as well.

Sentence 3 'To deal is to give out the cards to each player' tells the child the meaning instead of drawing it from the passage. It also points the child to 'he gathers them up', which is distractor D's content, without saying that gathering is not dealing.

It never reaches the meaning: it ends on 'give the betting conditions as the cause' without saying the conditions were 'so difficult to their friend', so they felt uneasy about whether it was fair. 'Line 77 says it was not the value of the stake' misstates 'not so much by the value of their stake'.

No step to the key. 'The list is about bodies in a game' is vague and does not show that a stitch is a pain from running, or rule out line 18's 'trick'. 'he knows who is tired' gives the narrator a gender the poem never states (the narrator is 'I').

The script lists lines 42, 43 and 44 and draws no conclusion, so it never shows that 'not shifting out of there' means not moving away from the goal. It brings in the stacking of jumpers (distractor C's content) without setting it aside. 'him/he' gives a gender to the poem's 'I' narrator. Question-level note: the key 'Moving himself' makes the same assumption.

It only rules out A and B ('Nobody gives him an instruction, and nothing is being put in a line'). It never shows that 'put his fur in order' means tidying it, and it leaves distractor C (wet and tangled mess) untouched.
It never links his asking 'Who is Nag?' to being new to the place. The last sentence ('Line 52 is Darzee explaining the trouble') is beside the point, so the script ends without reaching the key.

No step to the meaning. 'Line 8 says you can look it up' is irrelevant, and the script never uses lines 8-9 ('If you leave them in the net after that...') to show the wing-pumping tells you what will happen next.

'Line 31 says one went through the serving hatch': 'hatch' is on line 32. 'Line 31 is about the extinguisher instead' is muddled. It never shows that a serving hatch is an opening through to the kitchen.
It lists three facts from lines 24-25 and draws no conclusion, so it never shows that her temper 'got the better of her'. It points to the shaking (distractor C's content) without setting it aside.

It does not make the inference that the earlier 'warm spell' means the ice may be thin, so he is testing it. Sentence 1 points to skating along the shore (distractor D's content) without setting it aside.

No step to the key. Sentence 1 repeats distractor D's content ('put the fork in a hand's width back'). It never uses the 'knife going into an apple' noise to show spearing means pushing the point right through, as opposed to picking food up on a fork (distractor C).

It lists lines 25-26 and draws no conclusion that 'plot fourteen' is a numbered piece of growing ground (the potatoes, the marrow, the row). It points to 'the end of the row', which is distractor D's content.

Sentence 4 'Paler than his wont means paler than he usually looks' gives the meaning without showing how 'paler than his ...' signals a comparison with his normal look. Sentence 2 (the reply on line 12) is irrelevant.
No step to the key. It points to 'received me in silence' and stops, which pushes towards distractor C ('Completely silent'). It never shows what 'sullen' adds to the silence (resentment).
Line 3 'Swollen ... Wood swells' and lines 3-4 'every door ... stops shutting properly'; the script correctly draws 'grows bigger' from doors no longer fitting. Form ok.

It lists lines 17-18 and never draws the conclusion. It does not use 'hovered before they settled' to show they stayed up in the air before landing, as opposed to landing straight away (distractor C).
